content: Estradiol is the primary intracellular estrogen in humans and exhibits significantly greater potency at the receptor level compared to its metabolites, estrone and estriol. In premenopausal women with normal menstrual cycles, the ovarian follicle serves as the main source of estrogen, secreting between 70 to 500 micrograms of estradiol daily, depending on the phase of the menstrual cycle. Following menopause, the majority of endogenous estrogen is derived from the peripheral conversion of androstenedione, a hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex, into estrone. Consequently, estrone and its sulfate-conjugated form, estrone sulfate, become the most abundant circulating estrogens in postmenopausal women. Estrogens exert their effects by binding to nuclear receptors located in estrogen-responsive tissues. To date, two distinct estrogen receptors have been identified, and their distribution varies across different tissues. Circulating estrogens regulate the secretion of gonadotropins—luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)—from the pituitary gland through a negative feedback mechanism. In postmenopausal women, estrogens help to lower the elevated levels of these gonadotropins. Parenterally administered medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) inhibits gonadotropin production, thereby preventing follicular maturation and ovulation. However, available evidence suggests that this effect does not occur when MPA is administered orally at the typically recommended single daily dose. MPA may exert its beneficial effects on the endometrium partly by reducing nuclear estrogen receptor levels and suppressing epithelial DNA synthesis in endometrial tissue. Endogenous estrogens play a critical role in the development and maintenance of the female reproductive system and secondary sexual characteristics. While circulating estrogens exist in a dynamic equilibrium of metabolic interconversions, estradiol remains the most potent and principal intracellular estrogen.
